paragraphs: Learning from rare rewards can require an agent to interact with its environment millions of times. Hindsight Experience Replay makes unsuccessful attempts useful by changing the goal afterward: an attempt that missed its intended destination may still have achieved something else. Visual tasks complicate this strategy because success can depend on recognizable features in the images the agent sees.

The paper introduces a generative model that changes those observations so that recorded trajectories appear successful. The model learns from relatively few snapshots of the goal. Combining these altered visual experiences with hindsight replay gives reinforcement learning agents a way to reuse experience when simply changing a goal description would not suffice.

The authors evaluate the approach on three-dimensional navigation tasks and a simulated robotics application, reporting marked improvements over baselines drawn from earlier work. These findings support the usefulness of modifying visual observations to make hindsight replay applicable in the tested settings, extending its sample-efficiency motivation to image-based environments.
neurips-2019-addressing-sample-complexit.tldr: A generative model makes visual experiences appear successful so agents can benefit from hindsight replay in visual tasks.

paragraphs: Bats demonstrate that echoes can provide information about three-dimensional surroundings. This paper uses that observation to motivate a high-resolution imaging system that reconstructs target objects from ultrasound. Its central task is to turn recorded sound reflections into a spatial representation, providing an imaging route that does not depend on optical measurements.

The system combines a custom ultrasound acquisition module, called Bat-I, with a neural network called Bat-G. The inputs are echoes from hyperbolic frequency-modulated ultrasonic chirps. Within the network, an encoder emulates the bat's central auditory pathway, while a decoder converts the encoded information into a three-dimensional graphical representation of the target.

The authors report uniform reconstruction results, with precision of 0.896, recall of 0.899, and an F1-score of 0.895. Their experiments demonstrate the feasibility of implementing this bat-inspired, sound-based imaging approach. The contribution therefore joins specialized sensing hardware with a learned reconstruction system, showing how ultrasonic measurements can support the proposed three-dimensional imaging pipeline.
neurips-2019-bat-g-net-bat-inspired-high.tldr: Bat-G combines custom ultrasonic sensing with a bat-inspired neural network to reconstruct three-dimensional objects from echoes.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks estimate probability distributions while supporting attractive inference operations. Choosing their structure is harder to justify systematically than learning their numerical parameters: many existing methods rely on heuristic design choices. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework that treats learning the effective structure and learning the parameters as parts of one inference problem.

The approach separates the computational graph from its scope function, which determines the effective structure over that graph. Learning this function must preserve the network's completeness and decomposability requirements. For an important, widely used special case, the authors introduce structural parameters that can be included directly in Bayesian posterior inference.

Experiments show that Bayesian networks often achieve better test likelihoods than greedy structure learners. The framework also supports choosing hyperparameters through a Bayesian model score without a separate validation set, which matters when data are scarce. The authors additionally report consistent, robust structure learning with missing data and describe applicability to heterogeneous domains and extensions to nonparametric models.
neurips-2019-bayesian-learning-of-sum-pr.tldr: A Bayesian framework jointly learns sum-product network structure and parameters, often improving test likelihood and supporting missing data.

paragraphs: MNIST was derived from the NIST handwriting database, but the exact processing steps were no longer available. This paper reconstructs that derivation closely enough to produce a replacement dataset with insignificant accuracy changes. It also traces each MNIST digit back to its source, recovering associated information such as writer and partition identifiers.

The reconstruction yields a complete test set containing 60,000 examples, compared with the familiar 10,000. The other 50,000 had never been distributed. That makes them useful for examining whether many years of experimentation on the established benchmark have affected how well reported test performance reflects performance on additional digits.

The authors find that misclassification rates shift slightly, while the ordering of classifiers and the usefulness of model selection remain broadly reliable. They attribute this stability to comparing classifiers on the same digits, which provides paired comparisons. The result distinguishes the accuracy of a reported error rate from the reliability of a comparison between models.
neurips-2019-cold-case-the-lost-mnist-di.tldr: Reconstructing MNIST uncovers 50,000 undistributed test digits and finds that classifier rankings remain broadly reliable despite slight error-rate shifts.

paragraphs: Dense correspondence tasks require detailed visual matches, but human annotations for them have intrinsic inaccuracies. In DensePose, this makes the quality of supervision a central issue. The paper equips neural predictors to output distributions over labels, allowing them to represent uncertainty arising from annotation noise rather than producing only a single label prediction.

A key contribution is accounting for errors that vary together across the predicted field. The authors show that such correlated errors arise naturally in these applications and can be modeled by deep networks. This treats annotation uncertainty as structured information, giving the model a richer account of how labels can be unreliable.

The resulting models improve accuracy on the original DensePose task and establish a new state of the art on that benchmark. The uncertainty estimates also help combine predictions from multiple models, producing further accuracy gains. Thus, modeling supervision noise serves both the individual predictor and the process of deciding how to fuse several predictors.
neurips-2019-correlated-uncertainty-for-.tldr: Modeling correlated annotation uncertainty improves DensePose predictions and provides a principled way to combine multiple models.

paragraphs: Salient object detection identifies objects that stand out in an image. Training deep networks for this task with high-quality labels is expensive, so unsupervised approaches often obtain substitute labels from handcrafted saliency methods. Those substitutes contain noise, making the quality of the automatically generated supervision an important part of the learning problem.

DeepUSPS addresses this with two stages. First, a separate deep network learns to reproduce the pseudo labels from each handcrafted method. A self-supervision procedure then refines these labels incrementally over several iterations. Second, the refined outputs from the collection of networks become the training supervision for the final saliency detector.

This arrangement makes label refinement an explicit step before training the detector that will perform the task. Across the evaluated datasets, the authors report better performance than existing unsupervised methods, with results comparable to fully supervised state-of-the-art approaches. The findings show that iteratively improving noisy supervision can yield strong saliency predictions without the high-quality labels used by supervised methods.
neurips-2019-deepusps-deep-robust-unsupe.tldr: DeepUSPS iteratively refines automatically generated saliency labels before using them to train a strong unsupervised detector.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet allocation provides a way to discover interpretable topics in grouped data, but applying it to items beyond categorical observations remains challenging. Many richer datasets have a similar grouping structure. This paper introduces logistic LDA to make that topic-modeling approach easier to apply when the individual items take more general forms.

Logistic LDA is a discriminative variant that can handle groups of images, text embeddings, and models incorporating deep neural networks. Its central contribution is to accommodate these inputs while retaining the interpretability and principled motivation associated with LDA. The structure of the data remains central even as the representation of each item becomes more flexible.

Although the model is discriminative, the authors show that it can learn without labels by exploiting how items are grouped. This matters because richer input formats do not have to come with supervised topic assignments. The paper offers a route for bringing interpretable topic modeling to grouped observations that are awkward to represent as conventional categorical inputs.
neurips-2019-discriminative-topic-modeli.tldr: Logistic LDA uses group structure to learn interpretable topics from unlabeled, general-purpose inputs such as images and text embeddings.

paragraphs: Auditing a classifier requires understanding more than which inputs directly affect its predictions. A feature can also matter indirectly through other features that act as proxies. Influence can further differ between a particular person's prediction and the pattern across an entire dataset. The paper addresses these dimensions together through a procedure called disentangled influence audits.

The procedure uses disentangled representations to identify proxy features and explicitly calculate their influence. It supports both individual outcomes and aggregate outcomes, making it possible to ask which proxies matter for a specific prediction as well as which matter overall. This connects the detection of proxy information with an assessment of how the audited classifier uses it.

The authors support the approach with theory and experiments. They show that the audits can detect proxies and identify which ones most affect the classifier at either scale. The stated advance is a broader account of indirect feature influence, extending beyond approaches that concentrate on only one type or level of influence.
neurips-2019-disentangling-influence-usi.tldr: Disentangled influence audits identify proxy features and quantify their effects on individual predictions and aggregate classifier behavior.

paragraphs: A neural population can contain many signals, while only a small subset matters for the current task. Downstream circuits must identify that subset quickly to explain flexible behavior. Learning the relevant neurons through extensive supervised practice would be difficult to reconcile with the rapid task changes that humans and animals can manage.

The paper proposes that shared random modulation could help identify those neurons. Such modulation introduces noise and is preferentially directed toward task-informative neurons. The authors hypothesize that this seemingly harmful signal also labels useful information: a downstream decoder could use the strength of each neuron's modulation to determine how much to weight its activity.

In simulations of spiking neurons, a linear decoder whose weights approximate these modulation strengths achieves near-optimal accuracy. This supports the proposed mechanism for fast, task-dependent routing without predefined knowledge of the informative neurons or very large amounts of supervised training. The biological interpretation remains a hypothesis supported here by the simulated encoding and decoding system.
neurips-2019-flexible-information-routin.tldr: Simulations suggest shared neural noise can mark task-relevant neurons and enable rapid, accurate information routing.

paragraphs: Optimizing a model with many variables can be expensive. This paper proposes working in randomly chosen subspaces, extending the idea of coordinate descent beyond selecting individual coordinates. Its central choice is how to sample those subspaces: the proposed method adapts the sampling to the data instead of using an oblivious sampling scheme.

The adaptive subspaces come from correlated random matrices whose statistics reflect the input data. The authors show that the improvement in relative solution error can be tightly described using the spectrum of the data matrix, and they provide probabilistic upper bounds. They also illustrate how different patterns of spectral decay affect the theory's consequences.

Experiments report significant speedups for logistic regression, kernel classification using random convolution layers, and shallow networks with rectified linear units. The analysis uses convex analysis and Fenchel duality and connects the method to sketching and randomized matrix decompositions. Together, these results explain why data-informed random subspaces can improve optimization and demonstrate benefits on the tested learning problems.
neurips-2019-high-dimensional-optimizati.tldr: Data-adaptive random subspaces improve high-dimensional optimization, with spectral error bounds and substantial experimental speedups.

paragraphs: Reward machines represent a reinforcement learning reward function using an automaton, giving the task a structured decomposition into smaller problems. Those subproblems can be learned efficiently with off-policy methods. This paper shows how to learn reward machines from experience, removing the need for a user to specify that structure in advance.

The authors formulate the search for a reward machine as discrete optimization. The objective is to find a decomposition whose subproblems have optimal memoryless policies that combine into an optimal policy for the original task. This is especially relevant under partial observability, where choosing an action from the current observation alone may not capture the information needed for the whole problem.

Experiments in three partially observable domains show significant improvements over A3C, PPO, and ACER. The findings support learning useful task structure alongside behavior, rather than requiring the structure to be supplied beforehand. The contribution combines an explicit criterion for a useful decomposition with empirical evidence that learned reward machines can help solve the tested problems.
neurips-2019-learning-reward-machines-fo.tldr: Learning reward machines from experience provides task decompositions that improve reinforcement learning in three partially observable domains.

paragraphs: A dataset can contain overlapping groups whose predictive relationships differ substantially. A model trained across everyone may emphasize weak global patterns while missing strong local effects. This paper addresses that problem by learning a personalized model for every sample, aiming to support predictions and interpretations at the individual level.

The approach does not require a predefined network of similarities between samples. Instead, it uses covariates outside the modeled relationships to learn a latent distance metric over the samples. The resulting individual models can be examined for subgroup dynamics that are more detailed than broad class labels, fitting the paper's motivation of understanding heterogeneous populations.

The authors apply the method to simulated, financial, biomedical, and electoral data. They report fine-grained interpretations without losing predictive accuracy relative to state-of-the-art models such as deep neural networks. These findings indicate that, in the studied applications, personalization can reveal localized relationships while retaining strong prediction, rather than making interpretation depend on a single model shared by all samples.
neurips-2019-learning-sample-specific-mo.tldr: Sample-specific regression models reveal localized predictive relationships while matching strong predictive models in the evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Communication and correlated strategies can support socially better outcomes than Nash equilibria in multiplayer games. This paper studies coarse correlated equilibria in sequential games where players' interests need not be directly opposed. It separates two questions: how hard it is to find an equilibrium maximizing social welfare, and how learning algorithms can reach an equilibrium.

For games with at least three players, including chance, the authors prove that welfare maximization is not in Poly-APX unless P equals NP. They also show that counterfactual regret minimization using behavioral strategies may fail to converge to a coarse correlated equilibrium. Two new variants repair this: CFR-S constructs correlated strategies through sampling, while CFR-Jr uses a more involved reconstruction procedure.

Both variants have convergence guarantees. Across the experimental testbed, they compute coarse correlated equilibria dramatically faster than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. CFR-Jr also performs well as a heuristic for socially optimal equilibria. That empirical welfare result complements the convergence guarantee without establishing guaranteed welfare optimization.
neurips-2019-learning-to-correlate-in-mu.tldr: Two regret-minimization variants provably reach coarse correlated equilibria and compute them much faster in multiplayer game experiments.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses both labeled and unlabeled examples to train a classifier. MarginGAN introduces an adversarial framework with three components: a generator, a discriminator, and a classifier. Alongside the usual competition over whether generated examples look real, it adds a competition over the classification margins of those examples.

The discriminator learns to separate real examples from generated ones. The classifier tries to increase margins for real examples and decrease them for generated examples. The generator works in the opposite direction, seeking examples that both look realistic and receive large margins. Pseudo labels allow generated and unlabeled examples to participate in training.

This design connects the motivation of large-margin classification with adversarial generation, giving the generator two objectives to challenge simultaneously. Benchmark experiments report improved error rates and shorter training times. The authors also describe the approach as orthogonal to several state-of-the-art methods, indicating that its contribution can complement other approaches rather than depending solely on replacing them.
neurips-2019-margingan-adversarial-train.tldr: MarginGAN adds a classification-margin competition to adversarial training, improving semi-supervised error rates and training time in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Ranking agents is difficult when winning relationships form cycles and match outcomes are noisy. Elo cannot represent intransitive interactions, while some equilibrium-based alternatives face restrictions or computational obstacles. Alpha-Rank provides a tractable approach for general games, but evaluations commonly treat observed outcomes as if they were free of noise.

This paper studies ranking when information comes from noisy outcomes in games with many players and potentially different interests. It derives sample-complexity guarantees, addressing how much evidence is needed to rank agents confidently. The authors also propose adaptive ranking algorithms and establish correctness and sampling guarantees for those procedures.

Another contribution connects uncertainty about individual match outcomes with uncertainty about the resulting rankings. This makes the reliability of a ranking part of the evaluation problem itself. The approaches are evaluated on Bernoulli games, a soccer meta-game, and Kuhn poker. Together, the contributions provide a framework for reasoning about evaluation confidence when simulated matches supply incomplete and noisy evidence.
neurips-2019-multiagent-evaluation-under.tldr: Adaptive ranking algorithms and sampling guarantees support confident multiagent evaluation from noisy match outcomes.

paragraphs: Some guarantees for training oversized neural networks rely on parts of the network staying close to their random initialization. Holding those parts fixed explicitly yields learning with random features. This paper formalizes that connection and asks how much of neural-network learning such an explanation can account for.

The authors prove a limitation: for standard Gaussian inputs in dimension d and polynomially bounded target weights, random features cannot learn even a single ReLU neuron unless network size or weight magnitude grows exponentially with d. Since a single neuron is known to be learnable by gradient-based methods, success through random features does not fully explain the capabilities of those methods.

The paper also gives a self-contained random-feature proof that networks with one hidden layer can learn low-degree polynomials. The positive and negative results clarify both the usefulness and the scope of this theoretical viewpoint. Random features explain some successful learning behavior, while the stated lower bound identifies behavior that calls for a broader explanation.
neurips-2019-on-the-power-and-limitation.tldr: Random features explain some neural-network guarantees but face exponential requirements for learning even one ReLU neuron in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Policy optimization in a two-sided game can be difficult because one side seeks to increase an objective while the other seeks to decrease it. This paper studies zero-sum linear quadratic games through their policy-space optimization landscape. That landscape is neither convex nor concave, so its structure is important for understanding whether gradient methods reach an equilibrium.

The authors show that a stationary point of the objective with respect to linear feedback policies constitutes a Nash equilibrium. Building on this property, they develop three projected nested-gradient algorithms and prove that they converge to the equilibrium. Each method has a globally sublinear convergence rate and a locally linear rate.

Simulations illustrate the algorithms' convergence behavior, complementing the theoretical guarantees. The contribution establishes that this structured class of games admits provably successful policy optimization despite its nonconvex, nonconcave formulation. The authors position the work as an initial step toward understanding policy-based reinforcement learning in more general zero-sum Markov games, rather than a guarantee covering that broader class.
neurips-2019-policy-optimization-provabl.tldr: Three policy-gradient methods provably converge to Nash equilibria in zero-sum linear quadratic games.

paragraphs: Algorithm configuration searches for parameter settings that make a heuristic perform well on a distribution of problem instances. Earlier Structured Procrastination offered strong near-optimality guarantees and an anytime property: running it longer tightened its guarantees. However, it treated inputs according to the worst case. Another method gained adaptivity but gave up that anytime behavior.

Structured Procrastination with Confidence combines those properties. It preserves near-optimality and progressively improving guarantees while adapting to characteristics of the algorithm being configured. In particular, the authors show that it can run dramatically faster when many candidate configurations perform poorly, a condition that makes treating all candidates as worst cases unnecessarily costly.

Empirical results show that these favorable conditions occur frequently in practice. They also demonstrate the usefulness of the anytime property for finding good configurations quickly. The contribution therefore concerns both how efficiently the search responds to its candidates and how the quality assurances improve as more computation becomes available, without requiring a fixed stopping point to obtain useful results.
neurips-2019-procrastinating-with-confid.tldr: Structured Procrastination with Confidence combines adaptive configuration search with near-optimality guarantees that tighten as it runs.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning is often formulated as though the environment waits while an agent selects its next action. Real environments can keep changing during that computation. This paper examines the mismatch, which becomes especially consequential when learned controllers are applied in settings where the timing of actions matters for their outcomes.

The authors introduce a framework in which states and actions evolve simultaneously and establish its relationship to the classical Markov decision process formulation. They then analyze existing algorithms within this real-time framework, showing why those algorithms are suboptimal when used under its timing conditions. The analysis motivates a new method called Real-Time Actor Critic.

Real-Time Actor Critic outperforms Soft Actor Critic in both real-time and non-real-time settings in the reported results. This suggests that taking the interaction between computation and environmental change seriously can guide effective algorithm design. The paper's contribution includes both a formulation that accounts for simultaneous evolution and a learning algorithm developed from the shortcomings exposed by that formulation.
neurips-2019-real-time-reinforcement-lea.tldr: A framework for environments that evolve during action selection motivates Real-Time Actor Critic, which outperforms Soft Actor Critic in the reported settings.

paragraphs: A visual question answering model can sometimes answer correctly by exploiting patterns in the wording of a question, without examining the image. These shortcuts become a problem when question-answer relationships change between training and testing. RUBi is a training strategy designed to reduce this reliance on language-only biases in visual question answering models.

The method trains a question-only model to capture those biases. Its predictions influence the main model's predictions and dynamically adjust the training loss. Examples that are readily answered from the question alone receive less importance, encouraging the main model to draw on both the image and the question.

The authors evaluate RUBi on VQA-CP v2, which deliberately changes question biases between training and test data. They report results exceeding the previous state of the art on that benchmark. This supports the strategy's value under the tested distribution shift: identifying shortcuts with a separate model can help reduce how strongly those shortcuts guide the training of the full model.
neurips-2019-rubi-reducing-unimodal-bias.tldr: RUBi uses a question-only model to reduce language shortcuts during visual question answering training.

paragraphs: SPIDER provides near-optimal bounds on the number of first-order information queries needed for smooth nonconvex optimization. Its step size depends on the requested accuracy, however, which slows practical convergence, and it does not directly accommodate nonsmooth regularizers. SpiderBoost addresses both issues while preserving the favorable complexity guarantee.

The method permits a larger, constant-level step size. A proximal extension handles objectives combining nonconvex optimization with nonsmooth regularization and has a provable convergence guarantee. Its oracle complexity is O(min{n^(1/2) ε^(-2), ε^(-3)}), improving the previous state-of-the-art bound by a factor of O(min{n^(1/6), ε^(-1/3)}). These bounds describe the computational information required to attain the requested accuracy.

The authors also introduce a momentum scheme for the composite setting. It retains near-optimal oracle complexity in theory and produces substantial experimental improvements. The overall contribution connects strong query-efficiency guarantees with changes intended to improve practical progress, while extending the range of objectives the algorithm can handle.
neurips-2019-spiderboost-and-momentum-fa.tldr: SpiderBoost supports larger steps, nonsmooth regularization, and momentum while retaining near-optimal optimization complexity.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels can be noisy and unreliable, so inferring the true answer often requires collecting multiple judgments and combining them probabilistically. Existing approaches can make this aggregation computationally expensive, restrict the settings they handle, or provide insufficient theoretical assurance. This paper focuses on the case where each item has one of two possible classes.

The proposed algorithm, Streaming Bayesian Inference for Crowdsourcing, is designed to process this evidence with low computational complexity. Its streaming formulation allows use in a real-time online setting, making it suitable for updating classification inferences as crowd information arrives. Computational efficiency is therefore part of the algorithm's central contribution alongside its inference quality.

The authors report accuracy matching the best state-of-the-art algorithms across the settings considered. They also establish asymptotic guarantees for both online and offline use. These results connect efficient ongoing aggregation with theoretical support and competitive accuracy, addressing several weaknesses of earlier approaches within the paper's binary crowdsourced-classification problem.
neurips-2019-streaming-bayesian-inferenc.tldr: SBIC efficiently aggregates noisy binary crowd labels online while matching leading accuracy and providing asymptotic guarantees.

paragraphs: Interactive recommenders can learn detailed preferences from users' natural-language feedback. Yet exploring new items can lead a system to recommend something that contradicts a preference the user already expressed. This paper addresses the tension between gathering information through exploration and making recommendations consistent with the accumulated conversation.

The proposed framework augments reinforcement learning with a discriminator that detects violations of historical user preferences. That signal is incorporated into the usual objective of maximizing expected cumulative future reward. The approach gives past feedback a role in evaluating candidate recommendations as learning continues, rather than relying on reward maximization alone to account for those preferences.

The authors also extend the framework to constrained text generation, demonstrating that its formulation applies beyond recommendation. Empirical results show consistent improvements over standard reinforcement learning methods. These findings support incorporating a learned preference-violation signal into sequential decision making, while the stated aim is to reduce violations rather than guarantee that every generated recommendation satisfies every past preference.
neurips-2019-text-based-interactive-reco.tldr: A learned preference-violation detector augments reinforcement learning to improve interactive recommendations and constrained text generation.

paragraphs: Total least squares allows errors in both the input matrix and the target matrix. It seeks small corrections to both so that an exact linear relationship exists between the corrected matrices. This paper develops a faster approximate solver for the common overconstrained setting, where the number of rows greatly exceeds the other dimensions.

The algorithm finds coefficients whose correction cost is at most 1+ε times the optimum, plus an additive error η that can be an arbitrarily small function of n. Its runtime is approximately the number of nonzero input entries, plus a term polynomial in n/ε times d. Thus, beyond reading the input, the runtime does not directly depend on the potentially large row count.

The key is to solve for coefficients associated with an implicit corrected system instead of explicitly forming that system. This avoids the at-least-mn² cost of the discussed low-rank approximation route. The authors also extend the algorithm to regularized total least squares, broadening the scope of the computational result.
neurips-2019-total-least-squares-regress.tldr: An implicit-system algorithm approximates total least squares in input-sparsity time plus a smaller dimension-dependent term.

paragraphs: Time series can differ greatly in length, and useful labels are often scarce. This paper proposes an unsupervised method for learning general-purpose representations of such data. The aim is to produce embeddings for variable-length sequences with multiple measurements over time, while keeping the method scalable as sequences become longer.

The method combines an encoder built from causal dilated convolutions with a new triplet loss using time-based negative sampling. The encoder supplies the representation, while the training objective organizes learning through comparisons between examples. Together, these components provide a way to learn useful sequence descriptions without requiring labels for the training data.

The authors evaluate the representations through experiments and comparisons addressing their quality, transferability, and practical usefulness. These findings support the proposed embeddings as reusable descriptions of time series rather than representations tied only to a single labeled task. The central contribution brings unsupervised learning, variable-length multivariate inputs, and scalability with sequence length into one representation-learning approach.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-scalable-repre.tldr: Causal dilated convolutions and a time-based triplet objective learn scalable, transferable representations of unlabeled multivariate time series.
